feat(strategy): capture the checkpoint sync remote from tracked pushes

The single-remote election (ENT-1451) guesses the sync destination from
config at rest — origin, else sole, else first in .git/config — so a user
whose branches push a non-origin remote had checkpoints strand locally
until they hand-configured checkpoint_push_remote. First user report
landed the day after v0.10.0 shipped.

Capture makes the election follow demonstrated push behavior with zero
configuration: during pre-push, a push whose target agrees with the
branch's declared push destination (branch.<name>.pushRemote ->
remote.pushDefault -> branch.<name>.remote — the config a bare
'git push' resolves through) and differs from the current election
persists that remote as the captured election, announces it on stderr,
and the same push carries the checkpoints. The captured tier sits
between the explicit setting and origin, and is fail-soft: a captured
remote that was renamed or removed falls through to the default tiers
instead of disabling sync.

Neither signal elects alone. Declaration without a push is the
config-at-rest bug that got the static tracking tier dropped (74e239a9:
a 'clone -o base' stranded every origin push); a push without
declaration is the pre-single-remote transcript leak (a one-off
'git push upstream' must never publish transcripts). Capture acts only
on their intersection.

Phase-1 rules: at most one captured remote and the first capture sticks,

fix(strategy): scope empty-remote guard to configured remotes; document staleness limit

Addresses two trail-review findings on the local-ref guard:

- URL-push defers forever (fix): git hands the pre-push hook the bare URL as
  the remote arg when a push targets a URL directly (verified: $1 is the URL,
  not a name). git never records refs/remotes/<url>/*, so remoteHasTrackingRefs
  was always false → checkpoints deferred permanently for URL-push workflows.
  Guard now runs only when the arg resolves to a configured remote
  (isConfiguredRemote via `git remote get-url`, local/no-network); a bare-URL
  target publishes instead of stranding metadata. The first-branch hazard the
  guard exists for always uses a named remote, so no protection is lost. This
  also matches the reviewer's "…or default to origin" note.

- Recreated-empty-remote staleness (documented): a tracking ref left from before
  a remote was deleted and recreated empty under the same URL reads as
  "established", so v1 could publish to the now-empty remote. Detecting that
  needs a network round trip, which this design deliberately avoids; the earlier
  TTL only bounded a network probe's cache and no longer applies. Rare and
  recoverable — noted inline as an accepted limitation rather than reintroducing
  the network hit.

Test adds a bare-URL case asserting the guard publishes (does not defer).
